How MV games are made; smooth and efficient

Each module with its written-out name and its abbreviation. For a quick look while playing, FPS and frame time are usually enough; the others help to find out why a game stutters or gets slow. Colours: green = good (frame values only), yellow = getting close to a limit, red = past it; values without colour are fine. Frame values are judged against the chosen frame rate, so 30 fps is green when 30 fps is set.
How many images the game draws per second. RPG Maker MV games are made for 60; with the 60 fps limit the value should stay at 60. Lower values look less smooth.

Time between two images on screen, in milliseconds: 16.7 ms equals 60 fps, 33.3 ms equals 30 fps. The average shows the usual pace, max the longest gap. Green up to 1.25 target frames, yellow above, red from two target frames. The Frame graph module shows the same values over time.

The frame rate of the slowest 1 % of frames in the last update: it reveals stutter that an average hides. Slow counts frames that took longer than two target frames (33 ms at 60 fps, 67 ms at 30 fps).

Logic: game steps per second. MV runs its game logic at 60 steps per second, independent of the frame rate; fewer means the game itself runs slower. Hz: how often the screen asked for a new image; in brackets the refresh rate of the display.

How long the game\'s JavaScript needs per image (game logic and drawing commands). At 60 fps one frame has 16.7 ms; when this value gets close, the game cannot keep up. The graphics chip\'s work is not included.
Memory used by the game\'s JavaScript, and the limit the WebView allows. A value that keeps rising over a long session can point to a memory leak in the game; close to the limit the game may crash.
How many images the game keeps loaded (characters, tiles, pictures) and their size in megapixels. MV clears this cache itself; very high values cost memory.
Memory of the app itself (menus, overlay, on-screen controls). The game runs in Android\'s separate WebView process, so its memory shows under JS memory, not here.
Charge level, whether the phone is charging (+), and the battery temperature. Warm batteries (above about 40 °C) age faster, and phones often slow down when they are hot.

Android\'s own warning level for heat: none, light, moderate, severe, critical, emergency, shutdown. From moderate on, phones usually lower their speed, so the frame rate can drop. Heat: how close the phone is to severe throttling (100 %), as Android estimates it for the next seconds; not every phone reports it.
How the game is drawn (WebGL, WebGL 2 or Canvas, see Settings → Renderer) and the graphics chip the WebView uses. If WebGL 2 could not start, it says so.
Time of day, and how long you have been playing since this game was started (time in the app\'s menus counts, time with the app in the background does not).
Time the HUD itself needs per update to read and draw its values. It only runs when new values arrive and stays well below one millisecond.
The renderer decides how the game draws its pictures. WebGL is right for almost every game; the other two are alternatives for when something looks or runs wrong.
always try this first; it is how the game runs on PC too.
Fast, uses the graphics chip, and every effect works: lighting, fog, Mode 7 and filter plugins.
On a few devices the graphics driver has bugs, for example flickering or black pictures.
a game shows graphics errors, stays black or crashes with WebGL, or for very simple games without effects.
A simpler, very robust way of drawing that works the same almost everywhere.
Slower when many characters and effects are on screen; lighting, Mode 7 and filter plugins are missing or do not work.
WebGL causes problems on your device, or out of curiosity.
The newer version of WebGL; on some devices a little more stable or faster.
Experimental: the drawing library of RPG Maker MV games is made for WebGL 1, so usually you will not see a difference. If it cannot start, the app uses WebGL automatically.
A change applies the next time the game starts. The performance HUD (Renderer module) shows which one is running.
Saves battery; motion is less smooth

RPG Maker MV games always calculate their game logic 60 times per second. The frame rate only decides how many of those moments are drawn. The game runs at the same speed and the play time stays correct at every setting.
you play for a long time on battery or the phone gets warm.
Saves battery and keeps the phone cooler; the game itself is not slower.
Movement looks less smooth, most visible when walking or scrolling.
almost always; it is the default.
Exactly how MV games are made: every moment of the game logic is drawn once. Smooth without wasting power.
a game or plugin smooths motion between logic steps itself (rare), or for testing.
Draws as often as the screen refreshes, for example 120 times per second.
Experimental: with normal MV games the same picture is drawn twice without looking smoother, and the battery drains faster.
A change applies immediately, even during a game. The performance HUD shows the actual frame rate.
Frame times of the last seconds as a line

The frame times of the last few seconds as a line, newest on the right. Dashed lines mark the target frame time and twice that. Green up to 1.25 target frames (20.8 ms at 60 fps, 41.7 ms at 30 fps), yellow above, red from two target frames. Spikes are felt as stutter even when the fps value looks fine.
As large as possible; the aspect ratio stays.

The Canvas renderer has no shaders: only scaling, Pixel and colours apply.
Sharp, sharpening, scanlines and colour changes add one drawing pass per frame; the HUD shows what it costs.
MV games are drawn small (often 816 × 624) and enlarged to the screen. These options decide how.
Games with drawn or high-resolution art.

Edges and fine details stand out more clearly.
Too much adds bright halos at edges and makes noise visible; one extra drawing pass.
A retro look like an old TV.
Darker picture; looks best with integer scaling.

Every 15 minutes of play the app saves the game by itself, so stopping suddenly loses little. The game\'s own saves stay untouched.

How to add your own scripts to a game, step by step
Small JavaScript files that change a game, like a plugin does: show text at once, fix a bug, change a rule. The player runs them together with the game. Nothing in the game\'s own files is changed.
Patches can change anything in the game and read its data. Only use patches you trust.
Patches live in a folder called mvplayer-patches next to the game\'s index.html; in games made for Windows that is inside the www folder. The folder stays with the game when you copy it.
Open this guide from a game\'s settings to create the folder there with one tap.
This game has no patch folder yet.
The folder exists and holds %1$d files.
Folder created, with a short README inside.
That did not work. Is the game folder still shared with the app?
Put a .js file into the folder. Every .js file there runs after the game\'s plugins, in alphabetical order. Example:
Pick a file and add it
A file called patches.json chooses which scripts run and when. Then only the listed ones run:
Positions: beforeEngine (before everything), beforePlugins (before the first plugin), afterPlugins (after the last plugin, the default).

Start the game. The game\'s info card lists the patches it found under "Game patches". If a patch has an error, the game shows the error dialog; the diagnostic log names the script. To switch a patch off, rename it, e.g. to .js.off.
The saves you make in the game\'s own save menu, as its load menu shows them. They live in the game folder (www/save), like on PC. The app\'s auto saves are listed separately.
This game has no saves yet.
That did not work. Is it a zip of auto saves?
These auto saves belong to another game.

Put a mod\'s folder next to the game\'s www folder (or into a folder called mvplayer-mods) instead of copying it over the game. Switched on, its files are used instead of the game\'s; the game itself stays unchanged. Where several mods replace the same file, the upper one wins. Changes apply when the game starts.
No mods found. A mod is a folder with game folders such as data, js or img, or with a www folder holding them.
Mods can change the game\'s data: saves made with mods may not load without them.

Unpack the mod first (on PC or with a file manager app). Then put the unpacked mod folder, the one that holds the mod\'s own www folder, next to the game\'s www folder or into a folder called mvplayer-mods:

"Fear & Hunger/
├─ www/ ← the game
├─ BugFix Mod/ ← unpacked mod
│ └─ www/ …
└─ mvplayer-mods/ ← or in here
 └─ FnH-QoL-Patch/
 └─ www/ …"
Don\'t copy the mod\'s www folder over the game\'s. Then switch the mod on here.
Checking which files the mods replace…
No file is replaced by more than one active mod.
%1$d files are replaced by several active mods. The upper mod\'s file is used (bold); the others are ignored for that file. Core files decide whether the mods work together at all.
This deletes the folder “%1$s” with all its files from the game folder. This cannot be undone.

A mod changes a game by replacing some of its files: data, scripts, pictures or sounds. The player lays switched-on mods over the game and uses their files instead of the game\'s. The game\'s own files are never changed, and a mod can be switched off again at any time.
A mod can change anything in the game. Only use mods you trust.

Unpack the mod first (on a PC or with a file manager app); the player cannot open archives. Then put the unpacked mod folder, the one that holds the mod\'s own www folder, next to the game\'s www folder, or into a folder called mvplayer-mods:

Don\'t copy the mod\'s www folder over the game\'s: that would change the game for good. A folder with game folders such as data, js, img or audio counts as a mod, with or without a www folder inside. Mods stay with the game when you copy it.

Open the game\'s info card and tap Mods. Found mods are off at first. Switch one on to use it. Active mods are numbered: where several replace the same file, the upper one wins. Use the arrows to move a mod up or down.
Changes apply when the game starts. If the game is running, close it and start it again.

Below the list you see which files several active mods replace, and which mod wins. The files of the losing mods are ignored for that file. Mods made for the same game version usually fit together; mods that change the same data files need a decision from you: put the one you prefer on top.
Core files (js/rpg_*.js, js/plugins.js, index.html) are marked. Two mods that replace the same core file rarely work together; switch one of them off if the game breaks.
A file called mod.json in the mod folder (or in its www folder) gives the mod a name and details in the list:

scripts lists JavaScript files of the mod that run with the game, like game patches do. The path is relative to the www folder. Position is beforeEngine, beforePlugins or afterPlugins (the default). Without mod.json the folder name is the mod\'s name.

Mods can change the game\'s data, so saves made with mods may not load without them. Auto saves remember which mods were on; loading one made with different mods asks first. The game\'s own saves do not, so keep the same mods on while you play a save.
To remove a mod for good, use the trash button in the list: it deletes the mod\'s folder from the game folder after you confirm. To only pause a mod, switch it off.
